en: Howling in these days.
When Bakai bends over,
The flesh at his kneecaps parts;
When Bakai stoops,
His testicles are fully exposed.
His fur cap worn out, bareheaded,
Without a shirt, naked,
He is your poor Khan Bakai.
Meet him and become his companion;
He is your tiger, Bakai.
He is the hero who finds a way,
In place of your father, Khan Manas,
He is the lion who will support you.
Let me leave this here;
Again, my son, another tale—
Let me begin farther back.
Your cord-father Bölökbay—
Let me tell you of him.
The lame smith Bölökbay,
A star stirred in the heavens;
Your Bölök and David
Were friends unto the Last Judgment.
Putting all his skill into his work,
Taking counsel with David,
He made precious things.
Your father Manas, the lion,
Revealed his sacred worth;
A thousand young mares from his herds
He had given as his portion,
And made him khan of the treasury.
For your lordly, fierce father Manas,
He prepared his swords;
Gathering all the spears,
He made ready against the enemy.
Girding his waist firmly with gold,
Let me tell your Bölök's early story:
He was born in broad Crimea below.
Manas had the land searched,
The great felt cap, large as a yurt roof-cover—
He had brought from the hero Shuutu.
For your father, Sultan Manas,
He forged Zulpukor and brought it into being;
He made all his equipment ready.
Making Talas his homeland,
Completing all the equipment,
The lame smith Bölökbay
Made your father Manas strong.
The heroic smith Bölökbay
Came and settled in Talas,
Became a companion to your father Manas alone.
When your father died,
When the six villains came and divided the treasury,
He fought with gunfire for sixty days.
Divided, he was struck down.
Your father's forty companions
And the six leaders united;
Bölökbay lost the treasury.
The treasury of gold and silver,
Bölökbay left it scattered.
His forty companions beside him,
Leading his gray lamb,
Vanishing into the wilds,
Bölökbay fled.
He who was your cord-father,
Go and see Bölökbay;
Go and offer him your help.
Such is Bölökbay's story.
Let me leave this here;
Let me begin from this side.
Along broad Talas,
On the slopes of Kara-Too,
There are assembled judges;
There is your elder brother's house, the pig khan's.
Do not call that Talas a homeland;
Do not count your grandfather, the pig khan, as your people.
Malice waits in his eyes;
If he can, he stands ready to strike you down.
Crookedness lies in his eyes,
Deceit lies in his words.
If that old scoundrel finds his chance,
He stands ready to do you harm.
Do not lodge with him, calling him father;
Above all, do not eat his food.
If he feeds you, he will do you no good;
My orphan, he will not leave you unharmed.
In the pig khan's house
There is bozo in a leather bucket.
Do not drink it, my only one;
Burning poison is mixed inside.
There is bozo in a wooden vat,
In the house of your grandfather, that pig;
Choking poison is mixed in it.
Do not drink his bozo and swell up;
My little foal, do not meet with death.
Your grandfather, the pig khan's deeds—
His wickedness has reached far.
When your poor father died,
When I, disgraced, suffered torment,
You were still a babe in the cradle;
I was a desolate widow.
Since your father had died,
Not thirty days had passed.
That pig desired wickedness;
That pig called them to him
And urged his six sons on.
Raging and shouting,
He called his six sons:
'When a horse dies, you worthless men,
Its rump hide is needed;
When an elder brother dies, the younger
Needs his wife, you worthless men.
I have heard from those who came:
Six thousand ingots and a thousand beaver pelts,
Bakai has taken as a bribe;
Tekechi's Ormombek
Will help Kanykei escape, I have heard.'
Hearing it, they worked themselves into fury,
Abyke, Köbösh, the six villains,
Speaking in every manner.
They dug a deep pit for me;
Thus they boiled up my misery.
They put me to the test in widowhood,
Made it a reality upon my head.
The others were not so bad;
What began all the turmoil
Was your grandfather, the pig khan's treachery.
If you meet your grandfather, the pig khan,
Without fearing the sin of it,
Gouge his eyes blind;
Seize him and slaughter him;
Have him dragged along the road,
Slay him as a sacrifice.
Cut off his head and tie it up;
Bring it to me, your wretched mother!
Without letting it become unclean,
I will gouge out his two eyes,
Make a fried dish of them;
Bring him, and I will slaughter him.
The incurable pain, the heavy grief within me,
After that I will put them aside.
If I eat my fill of it,
Let the place that hurts in me grow quiet;
Let my eyes open wide.
Take the fitting course, my only one,
He is the support on whom to rely,
The heroic elder Bakai;
He is the hero who will find the way through this.
Such is your grandfather, the pig's story;
Let me finish telling this.
My fleet steed, my poor child, listen;
Now let me go farther on.
As you go on beyond there,
You will come to ridge after ridge,
To hilly land and mountain passes.
At the far edge of Talas,
On the side toward Ürbüz,
In the hollow of Kara-Too,
Along Kara-Zhar,
There are cowherds grazing cattle.
Among those cowherds,
She has a black milk cow with a torn nostril;
She has a torn black yurt.
He was your father's sworn brother;
When your father's sworn brother died,
When that hapless soul suffered torment,
Burulcha was left a widow—
Let me tell you of her.
She was the beauty among women;
Of the Chinese khan in Beijing,
She was Esen Khan's daughter.
From the events that passed,
Because of Burulcha,
Your mighty father died;
An army of four hundred twenty thousand died.
When they took Burulcha,
The beginning of the trouble grew fierce.
They fought six months without turning back;
In the end it was named the Great Campaign.
When they seized Burulcha,
When they went to that Beijing,
Many a devastating warrior went;
Twelve pairs of khans went;
Your father Manas, the lion, went;
Almambet and Chubak went together;
Azhibai and Khan Bakai went;
Men who could shatter the world went.
Into Beijing, untouched by the Flood,
They entered without stopping, raising strife.
Breaking the treasury, taking beauties,
As their prize, the champions
Took Birmyskal, Ai Zhang-zhung's daughter,
And Burulcha, Esen Khan's daughter,
Two outstanding maidens.
Into Beijing, untouched by the Flood,
They entered Beijing without stopping,
And held the khan's throne for nine months.
Where the Four Companions had never ventured,
They took Beijing city from Kakan.
Acting as though they would never die,
Your fierce father among them,
They feasted eighty days without ceasing.
Many people came among them,
To serve as imam;
Even the great imam of Mecca came.
Almambet and Chubak, the two lions,
Had the wishes of their hearts fulfilled.
Burulcha, Esen Khan's daughter,
Was married to Almambet.
Birmyskal, Ai Zhang-zhung's daughter,
'We took her as booty,' they said,
And had her married to Chubak.
Gold, silver, bright gold coins—
They left unable to load them all.
With the two maidens foremost,
Fair-faced young wives and beautiful maidens—
They left unable to gather them all.
Almambet and Burulcha
Settled there in Beijing.
For the space of nine months,
They lived as husband and wife.
When nine months were complete,
Bakai, great as a mountain, their guide,
Brought them to settle in Talas.
When Burulcha had come and settled in Talas,
When three months had passed since her arrival,
Akkula was struck by a bullet;
Almambet passed away a martyr.
Burulcha, Esen Khan's daughter,
Had turned toward the faith of Islam;
Then she lost my dear Almambet.
There Burulcha was left a widow.
Coveting her beauty,
The fool Abyke, one of the six villains, must have taken her.
She must have refused to yield herself to Abyke;
He must have beaten and flayed her.
This year he must have made her a neglected wife,
Subjected her to excessive humiliation.
Among the cowherds in the low ground,
Into the midst of those cowherds,
Giving her a black cow with a torn nostril,
Giving her a torn black yurt,
Making her work raw hides,
Putting her under the cowherds' rule,
He must have made her a milkmaid.
Upon your poor aunt by sworn kinship,
He must have avenged himself by beating her.
Her dress worn through and torn apart,
Bowl-sized patches of flesh showing,
If you do not go this year,
Your poor aunt by sworn kinship
Must have lost her dignity.
The hair at her temples is white.
If you do not go this year,
My little foal, it is her time to depart.
Weeping bitterly and sobbing,
Your mother is near death.
